reference.title: The Fun in Picking Sides [Planning & Game Design]
reference.method: Read the Japanese automatic transcript exported from the actual reference watch page; conceptual research only. Full transcript remains temporary, outside production assets.
reference.concept: A spectator needs someone or something to care about. Recognizable participants and a small choice can create a reason to follow an unfolding contest.
reference.scopeCorrection: Picking sides here is spectator allegiance, not branching fiction, faction alignment or a state-dependent story.

comparisons.existingQuestion: How do dialogue, item ownership, companions and completion state remain coherent across reordered actions?
comparisons.difference: Narrative state correctness and branch merging. The proposed video focuses on a non-playing viewer's reason to follow a contestant and the on-screen actions they can track.

comparisons.coverage: All revised chapters, including the closing checklist
comparisons.existingQuestion: How should the game acknowledge the player's own successful action without misleading or blocking the next action?
comparisons.difference: Recognition after one's own action; proposed topic is identification and suspense while watching another participant. Avoid recycling praise-strength comparisons.
comparisons.studioIdSource: Existing completed receipt; this review does not assert a new privacy check for that video.

comparisons.existingQuestion: How does a desired reward and visible progress suggest the player's next action?
comparisons.difference: Progress toward one's own acquisition and changed play after a reward. Spectator choice can work without awarding points or paying a reward; the new explanation will not repeat progression-bar design.

approvedScope: Spectator support and readable contest action: identify a contestant, offer a modest non-monetary reason to follow, keep identity stable as events unfold, show the meaningful risk and outcome, and test comprehension without claiming a measured increase in enjoyment.

refresh.comparison: Entire 34-scene current narration reviewed: independently implementing linked lists, falling blocks, collision/rotation/line clear, debugging, hint use and learning with AI. Does not explain spectator allegiance, stable participant identity, spectator selection, framing risk or reading competitive outcomes.
